Most master-master systems are either loosely consistent (violating ACID) or have increased write latency due to synchronization. Architecture planning task. Choose orchestration sub-phase order, evidence gates, system boundaries, risk review, and trade-off review. Treat the source note as architecture evidence only. Source=system-design-primer; Topic=Master-master replication. Evidence summary: There is a potential for loss of data if the master fails before any newly written data can be replicated to other nodes. Writes are replayed to the read replicas. If there are a lot of writes, the read replicas can get bogged down with replaying writes and can't do as many reads. The more read slaves, the more you have to replicate, which leads to greater replication lag. On some systems, writing to the master can spawn multiple threads to write in parallel, whereas read replicas only support writing sequentially with a single thread. Replication adds more hardware and additional complexity.

Source=system-design-primer; Topic=Federation. Evidence summary: Federation (or functional partitioning) splits up databases by function. For example, instead of a single, monolithic database, you could have three databases: **forums**, **users**, and **products**, resulting in less read and write traffic to each database and therefore less replication lag. Smaller databases result in more data that can fit in memory, which in turn results in more cache hits due to improved cache locality. With no single central master serializing writes you can write in parallel, increasing throughput.

Federation adds more hardware and additional complexity.

Index size is also reduced, which generally improves performance with faster queries. If one shard goes down, the other shards are still operational, although you'll want to add some form of replication to avoid data loss. Like federation, there is no single central master serializing writes, allowing you to write in parallel with increased throughput.

A sharding function based on consistent hashing can reduce the amount of transferred data. Joining data from multiple shards is more complex. Sharding adds more hardware and additional complexity.

Source=system-design-primer; Topic=SQL tuning. Evidence summary: MySQL dumps to disk in contiguous blocks for fast access. Use CHAR instead of VARCHAR for remediate-length fields. CHAR effectively allows for fast, random access, whereas with VARCHAR, you must find the end of a string before moving onto the next one. Use TEXT for large blocks of text such as blog posts. TEXT also allows for boolean searches. Using a TEXT field results in storing a pointer on disk that is used to locate the text block. Use INT for larger numbers up to 2^32 or 4 billion. Use DECIMAL for currency to avoid floating point representation operational risk. Avoid storing large BLOBS, store the location of where to get the object instead. VARCHAR(255) is the largest number of characters that can be counted in an 8 bit number, often maximizing the use of a byte in some RDBMS. Set the NOT empty value constraint where applicable to improve search performance.

Placing an index can keep the data in memory, requiring more space. Writes could also be slower since the index also needs to be updated. When loading large amounts of data, it might be faster to disable indices, load the data, then rebuild the indices.

The server response repeats the steps above in reverse order.
